stem: A cell of emf {{E}} V and internal resistance {{r}} Ω is connected across a {{R}} Ω resistor.
What current flows in the circuit?

hints.text: The current has to pass through two resistances. Where is the second one?
The internal resistance is in series with the external resistor.

ignores-internal-resistance.text: You divided by the external resistor only. The current also flows through the cell's own internal resistance, highlighted inside the cell.

only-internal-resistance.text: You used only the internal resistance. The current also passes through the external resistor.

dimension-mismatch.text: Current is measured in amperes. Check your unit.

generic.text: Add up every resistance the current passes through, then divide the emf by the total.

workedSolution.text: The cell's internal resistance r and the external resistor R are in series.
Total resistance = R + r = {{R}} + {{r}} = {{Rt}} Ω.

ignores-internal-resistance.front: A cell has emf E and internal resistance r. What current flows through an external resistor R?
ignores-internal-resistance.back: I = E/(R + r). The internal resistance is in series with R.

only-internal-resistance.back: Only when the terminals are shorted (R = 0). Otherwise I = E/(R + r).

generic.front: Current from a real cell into a resistor R?

stem: A cell of emf {{E}} V and internal resistance {{r}} Ω drives current through a {{R}} Ω resistor.
What does a voltmeter connected across the cell's terminals read?

hints.text: Is the voltmeter's reading the full emf while current flows? What happens inside the cell?
Find the current first, then subtract the voltage lost across the internal resistance: V = E − Ir.

terminal-equals-emf.text: The emf is the reading only when no current flows. With current flowing, some voltage is used up inside the cell. Watch the potential drop across r.

drop-across-internal.text: That is the voltage lost inside the cell (Ir). The voltmeter reads what is left: E − Ir.

added-internal-drop.text: The internal drop should be subtracted from the emf, not added. Potential falls across every resistance the current passes through.

dimension-mismatch.text: A voltmeter reads volts. Check your unit.

generic.text: Find the current, then subtract the drop across the internal resistance from the emf.

workedSolution.text: Current: I = E ÷ (R + r) = {{E}} ÷ {{Rt}} = {{I}} A.
Voltage lost inside the cell: Ir = {{I}} × {{r}} = {{drop}} V.
Terminal voltage: V = E − Ir = {{E}} − {{drop}} = {{V}} V. This equals IR across the external resistor.

steps.text: The voltmeter across the terminals reads the same as one across the external resistor.

terminal-equals-emf.front: When does a voltmeter across a cell read its full emf?
terminal-equals-emf.back: Only when no current flows. Otherwise it reads V = E − Ir.

drop-across-internal.front: What is Ir for a cell delivering current I?
drop-across-internal.back: The voltage lost inside the cell. The terminal voltage is E − Ir.

added-internal-drop.front: Terminal voltage of a cell delivering current: E + Ir or E − Ir?
added-internal-drop.back: E − Ir (while the cell is discharging).

generic.front: Terminal voltage of a cell with internal resistance r supplying current I?

stem: A vector of length r points at {{ang}}° above the x-axis.
Its x-component equals r times which ratio of {{ang}}°?

hints.text: Look at the x-shadow: is it opposite the angle or adjacent to it?
The x-shadow touches the angle at the origin, so it is adjacent.
adjacent = hypotenuse × cos θ.

sin-cos-swap.text: sin gives the side opposite the angle: here the y-component. The x-component is adjacent, so it uses cos.

tan-for-component.text: tan compares the two components (y ÷ x). It doesn't give a component from r.

generic.text: Decide whether the x-component is opposite or adjacent to the angle.

workedSolution.text: The vector is the hypotenuse; its x-shadow is adjacent to the angle at the origin.
adjacent = hypotenuse × cos θ, so x-component = r cos {{ang}}°.

sin-cos-swap.front: Vector r at θ above the x-axis: which ratio gives its x-component?
sin-cos-swap.back: cos θ: x = r cos θ (adjacent). y = r sin θ.

tan-for-component.front: What does tan θ tell you about a vector's components?
tan-for-component.back: tan θ = y ÷ x: it compares the components.

stem: In right triangle ABC the right angle is at C, and θ is the angle at {{at}}.
Which side is adjacent to θ?

hints.text: Two sides meet at the corner where θ is. One of them is the hypotenuse.
The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle: here AB. It is never called adjacent.
The adjacent side is the other side that touches θ's corner.

opposite-adjacent-confusion.text: That side is across from θ, so it is opposite. The adjacent side touches θ's corner.

hypotenuse-confusion.text: AB is the hypotenuse, the side opposite the right angle. Adjacent means the other side that touches θ.

generic.text: Look at the corner where θ is: which non-hypotenuse side touches it?

workedSolution.text: AB is the hypotenuse (opposite the right angle at C).
At corner {{at}}, the other side that touches θ is the adjacent side; the side across from θ is opposite.

opposite-adjacent-confusion.front: In a right triangle, which side is adjacent to an angle?
opposite-adjacent-confusion.back: The side that touches the angle and isn't the hypotenuse. The opposite side is across from it.

hypotenuse-confusion.back: No: the hypotenuse is the longest side, opposite the right angle.

generic.front: Opposite, adjacent, hypotenuse?
generic.back: Across from θ; touching θ; across from the right angle.

stem: In right triangle ABC (right angle at C), AC = {{a}}, BC = {{b}} and AB = {{c}}. θ is the angle at A.
What is {{fn}} θ? (A fraction such as 3/5 is fine.)

hints.text: Label the sides for θ at A: opposite, adjacent, hypotenuse.
sin = opposite ÷ hypotenuse; cos = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse; tan = opposite ÷ adjacent.
For θ at A: opposite = BC, adjacent = AC, hypotenuse = AB.

ratio-swap.text: You used the other side over the hypotenuse. Check which side is opposite θ and which is adjacent.

ratio-inverted.text: Your fraction is upside down. Each ratio has the hypotenuse (or, for tan, the adjacent side) on the bottom.

generic.text: Name the sides relative to θ, then pick the ratio's two sides.

workedSolution.text: For θ at A: opposite = BC = {{b}}, adjacent = AC = {{a}}, hypotenuse = AB = {{c}}.
{{fn}} θ = {{text}}.

ratio-swap.front: sin θ or cos θ: which uses the side adjacent to θ?
ratio-swap.back: cos θ = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse; sin θ = opposite ÷ hypotenuse.

ratio-inverted.back: No: sin θ = opposite ÷ hypotenuse (always at most 1).

generic.front: SOH CAH TOA?
generic.back: sin = O/H, cos = A/H, tan = O/A.

stem: Find ∫ ({{A3}}x² {{B2|signed}}x {{c|signed}}) dx.

hints.text: Integration undoes differentiation: you need a function whose derivative is the integrand.
∫ xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹ ÷ (n + 1) + C. Raise the power, then divide by the new power. The antiderivative measures the area building up under the curve.
∫ {{A3}}x² dx = {{a}}x³. Do the same for the other two terms.

forgot-to-divide.text: After raising each power by one, divide by the new power: ∫ x² dx = x³/3. Differentiate your answer to check: it should give back the integrand.

differentiated-instead.text: That's the derivative of the integrand, not its antiderivative. Integration raises powers; differentiation lowers them.

constant-term-not-integrated.text: The constant {{c}} integrates to {{c}}x, not {{c}}: its antiderivative must have derivative {{c}}.

generic.text: Check by differentiating your answer: it must give back the integrand exactly. Your curve (dashed, coral) is compared with the true antiderivative after the solution.

workedSolution.text: Integrate term by term with ∫ xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1).
So ∫ f dx = {{a}}x³ {{b|signed}}x² {{c|signed}}x + C. The solid amber curve is this antiderivative with C = 0.

forgot-to-divide.back: x³/3 + C: raise the power, then divide by the new power.

differentiated-instead.front: Integration vs differentiation: which raises powers?
differentiated-instead.back: Integration raises the power by one; differentiation lowers it.

generic.front: How can you check an antiderivative?
generic.back: Differentiate it: you should get the integrand back.

template.intro: This question helps us find the best place for you to begin.
stem: A cyclist's velocity rises steadily from {{u}} m/s to {{v}} m/s over {{t}} s, as the velocity–time graph shows.
How far does the cyclist travel in those {{t}} seconds?

hints.text: On a velocity–time graph, what does the area under the line stand for?
Split the region under the line into a rectangle and a triangle.
Rectangle: {{u}} × {{t}}. Triangle: ½ × ({{v}} − {{u}}) × {{t}}. Add them.

area-uses-final-velocity.text: {{v}} m/s × {{t}} s assumes the cyclist moved at the final speed the whole time. The coral region is what you counted; the cyclist only covered the orange area under the line.

area-ignores-acceleration.text: {{u}} m/s × {{t}} s is only the rectangle under the starting speed. The cyclist sped up, so the coral triangle on top counts too.

area-misses-rectangle.text: That's only the triangle. The cyclist was already moving at the start, so the coral rectangle underneath counts as well.

slope-instead-of-area.text: That's the slope of the line (rise over run), which is the acceleration. Distance is the area under a velocity–time graph, not its slope.

dimension-mismatch.text: Distance is a length. Check your unit.

unit-conversion-error.text: Check your unit conversion. The graph uses metres and seconds.

generic.text: Distance on a velocity–time graph is the area under the line. Which shapes make up that area?

workedSolution.text: Displacement equals the area under the velocity–time graph from 0 to {{t}} s.
Rectangle under the starting speed: {{u}} m/s × {{t}} s = {{rect}} m.
Triangle for the gain in speed: ½ × ({{v}} − {{u}}) m/s × {{t}} s = {{tri}} m.
Total distance: {{rect}} + {{tri}} = {{s}} m.

steps.text: For steady acceleration the average velocity is halfway between the start and end: ({{u}} + {{v}})/2 = {{(u+v)/2}} m/s.
Distance = average velocity × time = {{(u+v)/2}} × {{t}} = {{s}} m. The rectangle under the average-velocity line has the same area as the region under the graph.

area-uses-final-velocity.front: Velocity rises from u to v in time t. Why isn't the distance v × t?
area-uses-final-velocity.back: The body was slower earlier. Distance is the area under the v–t line: rectangle u·t plus triangle ½(v − u)t.

area-ignores-acceleration.front: Speeding up from u to v: is the distance u × t?
area-ignores-acceleration.back: No. That is only the rectangle. Add the triangle ½(v − u)t for the speed gained.

area-misses-rectangle.front: Which shapes make up the area under a rising v–t line that starts at u > 0?
area-misses-rectangle.back: A rectangle u·t under the starting speed plus a triangle ½(v − u)t on top.

slope-instead-of-area.front: On a v–t graph, what do the slope and the area tell you?
slope-instead-of-area.back: Slope = acceleration. Area under the line = displacement.

generic.front: How do you get distance from a velocity–time graph?
generic.back: Find the area under the line between the two times.

template.intro: This question helps us find the best place for you to begin.
stem: A car moving at {{u}} m/s brakes with a steady deceleration of {{a}} m/s².
How far does it travel from the moment the brakes are applied until it stops?

hints.text: You know the starting speed, the final speed and the deceleration. Which equation links those three with distance and leaves out time?
The distance is the area under the velocity–time graph. Use v² = u² − 2as, with v = 0 when the car stops.
0 = {{u}}² − 2 × {{a}} × s. Solve for s.

missing-half.text: That distance is twice too large: it is what the car would cover at {{u}} m/s for the whole stopping time (the dashed car). The real car slows down, so its average speed is only half the starting speed.

dropped-square.text: The starting speed should be squared. Stopping distance grows with the square of speed.

time-instead-of-distance.text: That number is the stopping time (u ÷ a), not the distance.

dimension-mismatch.text: Distance is a length. Check your unit.

unit-conversion-error.text: Check your unit conversion: the speeds are in metres per second.

generic.text: Try the equation that links speeds, deceleration and distance without time. The car now brakes so that it stops at your flag: compare the deceleration that needs with the {{a}} m/s² the brakes really give.

workedSolution.text: The car stops, so its final speed v = 0. Time isn't given, so use v² = u² − 2as.
Check: it stops after t = u/a = {{T}} s at an average speed of {{half}} m/s, and {{half}} × {{T}} = {{s}} m.

steps.text: Time to stop: t = u ÷ a = {{u}} ÷ {{a}} = {{T}} s.
Distance = area under the v–t graph = ½ × {{u}} × {{T}} = {{s}} m.

missing-half.front: Braking from u to rest: is the distance u × t?
missing-half.back: No. The speed falls steadily, so the average speed is u/2 and the distance is u²/(2a).

dropped-square.front: If a car's speed doubles, what happens to its stopping distance at the same deceleration?
dropped-square.back: It becomes four times as large: s = u²/(2a).

time-instead-of-distance.front: What do u/a and u²/(2a) give for a car braking to rest?
time-instead-of-distance.back: u/a is the stopping time; u²/(2a) is the stopping distance.

generic.front: Which equation gives stopping distance without the time?
generic.back: v² = u² − 2as with v = 0, so s = u²/(2a).

stem: f(x) = {{a}}x² {{b|signed}}x
Find f′(x).

hints.text: Move P to a few places and note the slope of the tangent. What pattern do you see?
The derivative's value at each x is the tangent's slope there. The dots mark those slopes.
Use d/dx(xⁿ) = n xⁿ⁻¹ on each term.

power-rule-forgot-multiply.text: When you differentiate x², bring the power down as a multiplier: d/dx(x²) = 2x. The dashed line uses your f′ as the tangent at P: it cuts across the curve instead of just touching it.

dropped-linear-term.text: The term {{b}}x also changes with x; its derivative is {{b}}. The dashed line uses your f′ as the tangent at P: it doesn't just touch the curve.

power-not-reduced.text: After bringing the power down, reduce it by one: d/dx(x²) = 2x¹, not 2x².

generic.text: The dashed line uses your f′(x) as the slope at P. A correct derivative gives a line that just touches the curve there. Move P and look again.

workedSolution.text: The derivative at each x is the slope of the tangent there.
Power rule: d/dx({{a}}x²) = {{two_a}}x and d/dx({{b}}x) = {{b}}.
So f′(x) = {{dref}}. Its graph passes through every slope dot.

steps.text: f′(x) = lim (h → 0) [f(x + h) − f(x)] ÷ h. Watch the secant become the tangent at x = 1.

power-rule-forgot-multiply.back: 2ax: bring the power down and reduce it by one.

dropped-linear-term.back: b, a constant (the slope of the line y = bx).

generic.front: What does f′(a) mean on the graph of f?
generic.back: The slope of the tangent at x = a.

template.intro: A quick check on turning.
stem: A car drives round a flat, level curve of radius {{r}} m at a steady {{v}} m/s.
Which force pulls the car towards the centre of the curve?

hints.text: Turning means accelerating towards the centre, so some real force must point that way. Which forces does the car feel, and from what agents?
On a level road the weight and the normal force are both vertical. Can a vertical force pull the car sideways?
Only the road's grip on the tyres can act sideways, towards the centre.

centrifugal-force-real.text: No agent pushes the car outward. What you feel as being 'thrown out' is your body continuing straight (inertia) while the car turns.

tangential-force-provides-centripetal.text: The engine's force acts along the direction of travel. It can change the speed, but not the direction.

normal-provides-centripetal.text: On a level road the normal force is vertical, so it can't pull the car sideways. (On a banked road it can help.)

generic.text: Find the force that points towards the centre and has a real agent.

workedSolution.text: Vertically, weight and normal force balance: the car neither rises nor sinks.
To turn, the car needs a net force towards the centre: here only the road's friction on the tyres acts sideways. Without grip (ice), the car would slide straight on.

centrifugal-force-real.front: Is there an outward 'centrifugal force' on a turning car?
centrifugal-force-real.back: Not in the road's frame of reference: no agent supplies it. The inward friction is what turns the car.

tangential-force-provides-centripetal.front: Can a forward driving force make a car turn?
tangential-force-provides-centripetal.back: No. A force along the motion changes speed; turning needs a force towards the centre.

normal-provides-centripetal.front: On a level curve, does the normal force turn the car?
normal-provides-centripetal.back: No, it is vertical. Sideways friction does.

generic.front: What turns a car on a flat road?
generic.back: Sideways static friction from the road, towards the centre.

args.text: Nothing pushes the car outward: no agent supplies a 'centrifugal force'.

template.intro: A banked curve: no friction needed at the right speed.
stem: A road curve of radius {{r}} m is banked at {{theta}}° so that a car can take it with no sideways friction at one particular speed. Take g = 9.8 m/s².
What is that speed?

hints.text: With no friction, only the weight and the normal force act. Which of them has a part towards the centre?
Split N: vertically N cos θ balances m g; horizontally N sin θ supplies m v² ÷ r.
Divide the two equations: tan θ = v² ÷ (r g), so v = √(r g tan θ).

banked-used-sin.text: Dividing N sin θ = m v²/r by N cos θ = m g gives tan θ, not sin θ.

tan-inverted.text: Check which equation is on top: horizontal ÷ vertical gives tan θ = v² ÷ (r g).

forgot-square-root.text: r g tan θ is v². Take its square root.

dimension-mismatch.text: Give a speed, in m/s.

generic.text: Resolve the normal force vertically and horizontally, then divide the two equations.

workedSolution.text: Only weight and the normal force act. Split N into vertical and horizontal parts.
Vertically: N cos θ = m g. Horizontally (towards the centre): N sin θ = m v² ÷ r.
Dividing: tan θ = v² ÷ (r g), so v² = {{r}} × 9.8 × tan {{theta}}° = {{v2}} and v = {{v}} m/s.

banked-used-sin.front: Banked curve, no friction: which trig ratio links v and θ?

tan-inverted.front: Is tan θ = r g ÷ v² for a banked curve?
tan-inverted.back: No: tan θ = v² ÷ (r g) (horizontal ÷ vertical).

forgot-square-root.front: μ g r for a level bend gives what?
forgot-square-root.back: v², the square of the greatest speed. Take the square root.

generic.front: Design speed of a banked curve?

template.intro: How fast can the car take the bend?
stem: A car takes a flat, level bend of radius {{r}} m. The coefficient of static friction between the tyres and the road is {{mu}}. Take g = 9.8 m/s².
What is the greatest speed at which it can take the bend without skidding?

hints.text: Friction is the only force towards the centre. What is the most friction the road can provide?
At the limit, μ m g = m v² ÷ r. The mass cancels.
v² = μ g r; take the square root.

forgot-square-root.text: μ g r is v², in m²/s². Take its square root to get the speed.

centripetal-without-friction.text: Only friction pulls the car inward, and at most it is μ m g. Your speed would need more grip than the road has.

dimension-mismatch.text: Give a speed, in m/s.

generic.text: Set the largest friction, μ m g, equal to the force needed to turn, m v² ÷ r.

workedSolution.text: Vertically: N = m g. The largest sideways friction is μ N = μ m g.
That friction must supply m v² ÷ r. At the limit, μ m g = m v² ÷ r, so v² = μ g r = {{v2}} m²/s².
v = √{{v2}} = {{v}} m/s (about {{kmh}} km/h). Any faster and the tyres skid outward.

forgot-square-root.front: μ g r for a level bend gives what?
forgot-square-root.back: v², the square of the greatest speed. Take the square root.

centripetal-without-friction.front: What limits the speed on a level bend?

generic.front: Greatest speed on a level bend?
generic.back: v = √(μ g r), independent of mass.

stem: Blocks A ({{m1}} kg) and B ({{m2}} kg) on a smooth floor are joined by a light string. A horizontal pull of {{F}} N acts on A, and both move together.
What is their acceleration?

hints.text: The string keeps the blocks together, so they share one acceleration.
Treat A, B and the string as one system. The tension is internal; the only external horizontal force is the pull.
a = F ÷ (m_A + m_B).

connected-only-one-mass.text: The pull has to accelerate both blocks, because the string drags B along. Use the total mass.

force-times-mass.text: Multiplying gives the wrong units. a = F ÷ total mass.

dimension-mismatch.text: Acceleration is in m/s².

generic.text: One system, one acceleration: divide the external force by the total mass.

workedSolution.text: System A + B: external horizontal force {{F}} N, total mass {{M}} kg.
a = {{F}} ÷ {{M}} = {{a}} m/s². (The string's tension, {{T}} N, only matters if you look at B alone.)

connected-only-one-mass.front: A pull on A drags B by a string. Which mass sets the acceleration?

force-times-mass.front: Net force F on mass m: acceleration?
force-times-mass.back: a = F ÷ m, not F × m.

stem: Masses of {{m1}} kg and {{m2}} kg hang on either side of a light, frictionless pulley, joined by a light string. They are released from rest. Take g = 9.8 m/s².
What is the size of their acceleration?

hints.text: Both masses move together, one up and one down, with the same size of acceleration.
Along the string, the net force on the system is the difference of the two weights. The tension is internal.
a = (m₁ − m₂) g ÷ (m₁ + m₂).

connected-only-one-mass.text: The net force moves both masses, so divide by m₁ + m₂, not by one mass.

atwood-free-fall.text: The lighter mass holds the heavier one back through the string, so the acceleration is less than g.

dimension-mismatch.text: Acceleration is in m/s².

generic.text: Net force along the string ÷ total mass.

workedSolution.text: Along the string, the heavier weight ({{W1}} N) pulls one way and the lighter ({{W2}} N) the other. Net force: {{dW}} N.
Both masses ({{M}} kg) accelerate together: a = {{dW}} ÷ {{M}} = {{a}} m/s². The tension is {{T}} N.

atwood-free-fall.front: Do the masses on a pulley fall with acceleration g?
atwood-free-fall.back: No: a = (m₁ − m₂) g ÷ (m₁ + m₂), less than g.

stem: Block A ({{mA}} kg) is tied by a light string to block B ({{mB}} kg). A hand pulls B with {{F}} N along a smooth table, so both blocks accelerate together.
Match each force acting on block A to the body that exerts it.
template.answerText: Weight → the Earth; normal force → the table; tension → the string

hints.text: A force on A must come from something touching A, or from the Earth's gravity.
What is actually attached to block A? The hand isn't touching it.
The string pulls A with tension T = {{T}} N, which is less than the hand's {{F}} N.

tension-from-hand.text: The hand touches block B, not A. Block A is pulled by the string, and that pull ({{T}} N) is smaller than the hand's {{F}} N because the string only has to accelerate A.

tension-agent-confusion.text: Block B doesn't touch block A: the string between them does the pulling. The string pulls A forward and pulls B backward.

normal-from-earth.text: The normal force is a contact force from the surface A rests on: the table.

weight-from-surface.text: Weight is the Earth's gravitational pull. The table pushes up with the normal force instead.

Normal force: the table pushes up on A.

tension-from-hand.front: A hand pulls block B, which pulls block A by a string. Who exerts the forward force on A?
tension-from-hand.back: The string. Its tension is smaller than the hand's pull (T = m_A a).

tension-agent-confusion.front: Two blocks joined by a string: does block B push or pull block A directly?
tension-agent-confusion.back: No. They don't touch. The string pulls each block toward the other.

normal-from-earth.front: Which body exerts the normal force on a block resting on a table?
normal-from-earth.back: The table (a contact force from the surface).

stem: A {{m}} kg box slides to the right across a rough floor (μ = {{mu}}). The push that started it has ended. Take g = 9.8 m/s².
Draw every force acting on the box now.
template.answerText: Weight {{W}} N down, normal {{W}} N up, friction {{f}} N to the left.

hints.text: List what touches the box now: only the floor. Gravity acts too.
The floor gives two forces: one perpendicular to it and one along it, opposing the sliding.
Weight down, normal up (equal here), friction μN to the left. The push has ended, so it is not on the diagram.

extra-force-of-motion.text: Nothing is pushing the box now. It keeps moving by inertia while friction slows it. Every arrow needs an agent touching the box (or gravity).

missing-weight.text: Every body near the Earth has a weight, mg, straight down.

missing-normal.text: The floor pushes up on the box; without it the box would sink.

The floor: a normal force {{W}} N up, and kinetic friction μN = {{f}} N to the left, opposing the sliding.
Nothing else touches the box. The net force is friction alone, so the box slows down. Press Play.

stem: A {{m}} kg box is pulled across a rough floor by a rope at {{ang}}° above the horizontal. The rope's tension is {{T}} N and the box moves at a constant 1.5 m/s. Take g = 9.8 m/s².
Draw every force acting on the box, with its direction and size.
template.answerText: Weight {{W}} N down (Earth); normal force {{N}} N up (floor); tension {{T}} N at {{ang}}° (rope); friction {{f}} N backwards (floor)

hints.text: List what touches the box: the floor and the rope. Gravity acts too. Each gives one or two forces.
Constant speed means the net force is zero. Watch the amber net-force arrow and press Play: the box should neither speed up nor slow down.
Vertically: N + T sin {{ang}}° = mg. Horizontally: friction = T cos {{ang}}°.

missing-normal.text: Without the normal force, your diagram predicts the box sinks through the floor: watch it drift away from the real box. The floor pushes up on the box.

missing-weight.text: Every body near the Earth has a weight, pulling straight down.

missing-tension.text: The rope pulls the box along its own direction, {{ang}}° above the horizontal.

missing-friction.text: Without friction, the rope's forward pull would make the box speed up, as your prediction shows. The rough floor opposes the sliding.

extra-force-of-motion.text: The box keeps moving because of inertia; there is no separate 'force of motion', and nothing pushes it. Every force needs an agent touching the box (or gravity).

normal-equals-weight.text: The rope pulls partly upward, so the floor doesn't need to push as hard: N = mg − T sin {{ang}}° = {{N}} N.

constant-velocity-unbalanced.text: At constant velocity the forces balance, so friction equals the rope's horizontal pull, T cos {{ang}}° = {{f}} N. Your prediction shows the box speeding up or slowing down.

normal-direction.text: The normal force is perpendicular to the floor, straight up.

tension-direction.text: Tension acts along the rope, at {{ang}}° above the horizontal.

friction-direction.text: Friction on a sliding box points opposite its motion, backwards.

double-counted-force.text: Each agent gives each kind of force only once. Remove the duplicate.

force-direction.text: Check the direction of each force.

force-magnitude.text: Check the sizes: constant speed means the forces balance.

extra-force.text: One of your forces has no matching interaction. Check every force has a real agent.

generic.text: Press Play: if the forces are right, the box keeps moving at a constant speed.

workedSolution.text: Weight: {{W}} N straight down, from the Earth.
Tension: {{T}} N along the rope, {{ang}}° above the horizontal.
Normal force: the forces balance vertically, so N = mg − T sin {{ang}}° = {{N}} N, up.
Friction: the forces balance horizontally, so f = T cos {{ang}}° = {{f}} N, backwards. The net force is zero: press Play to see constant velocity.

missing-normal.front: A box on a floor: which force stops it sinking into the floor?
missing-normal.back: The normal force from the floor, perpendicular to the surface.

missing-friction.front: A box pulled at constant speed on a rough floor: what balances the pull?
missing-friction.back: Kinetic friction from the floor, opposite the motion.

extra-force-of-motion.front: Is there a 'force of motion' on a moving box?
extra-force-of-motion.back: No. Motion continues by inertia; only forces with agents act.

normal-equals-weight.front: A rope pulls a box partly upward. Is N = mg?
normal-equals-weight.back: No. N = mg − T sin θ: the rope carries part of the weight.

constant-velocity-unbalanced.front: Constant velocity: what is the net force?
constant-velocity-unbalanced.back: Zero. All forces balance (Newton's first law).

missing-weight.front: Which force acts on every body near the Earth?

missing-tension.front: Which way does a rope pull?
missing-tension.back: Along the rope, away from the body.

generic.front: Steps for a free-body diagram?
generic.back: Gravity first, then one force per contact; check the net force matches the motion.

stem: An ice-hockey puck slides across perfectly smooth ice at a steady {{v}} m/s.
What net (resultant) force is needed to keep it moving at this speed?

hints.text: What happens to the speed if the net force is zero? Press Play.
A net force would change the velocity: speed it up, slow it down or turn it.
Constant velocity means the net force is zero (Newton's first law).

motion-needs-net-force.text: A net force changes velocity. With your force the puck would speed up, as the dashed puck shows. At a steady speed the forces balance; no force is needed just to keep moving.

generic.text: Ask what a net force would do to the motion.

workedSolution.text: Vertically the weight and the normal force balance. On smooth ice there is no friction.
The net force is zero, so the velocity doesn't change: the puck keeps sliding at {{v}} m/s. Press Play.

motion-needs-net-force.front: Does a body need a net force to keep moving at constant velocity?
motion-needs-net-force.back: No. Zero net force means constant velocity (Newton's first law).

generic.front: Constant velocity: net force?

options.text: No net force: the forces on it balance
A small forward force, to keep it going
A forward force proportional to its speed
A backward force, because moving things slow down

stem: A {{m}} kg box slides to the right at {{v0}} m/s across a rough floor. Your push has already ended.
Which forces act on the box now?
template.answerText: Weight, the normal force and friction pointing left

hints.text: A force needs an agent: something touching the box, or the Earth's gravity. What is touching the box now?
Add a Push to the right, press Play, and watch the speed. Does a sliding box on a rough floor really speed up?
The box is slowing down. Slowing down needs a net force pointing backwards.

extra-force-of-motion.text: Once your hand leaves the box, your push stops acting. Nothing pushes the box forward: it keeps moving because of inertia. The dashed box shows what your choice predicts; a real box slows down.

missing-friction.text: Without friction, nothing would slow the box: the dashed box keeps sliding at a constant speed. The rough floor exerts friction against the motion.

generic.text: List only forces with an agent touching the box now, plus gravity. Then ask whether those forces explain the box slowing down.

workedSolution.text: Agents acting on the box now: the Earth (gravity) and the floor (contact). Your hand is no longer touching it.
The floor pushes up (normal force) and rubs against the motion (friction, pointing left).
Net force: friction of {{f}} N to the left, so the box decelerates at {{f/m}} m/s² and slows down. Press Play to watch.

extra-force-of-motion.front: A box slides after you stop pushing. Is your push still a force on it?
extra-force-of-motion.back: No. Every force needs an agent in contact (or a field). The box keeps moving because of inertia, and friction slows it.

missing-friction.front: What slows a box sliding across a rough floor?
missing-friction.back: Kinetic friction from the floor, pointing opposite the motion.

generic.front: How do you decide which forces act on a body?
generic.back: Find each agent: things in contact with it, plus gravity. No agent, no force.

options.text: Its weight (from the Earth), the normal force (from the floor) and friction from the floor, pointing left
Its weight, the normal force, friction pointing left, and the force of your push pointing right
Its weight, the normal force and a forward “force of motion” that keeps it going

stem: A {{m}} kg block rests, without moving, on a rough plank tilted at {{theta}}°. Take g = 9.8 m/s².
Draw every force acting on the block, with its size and direction.
template.answerText: Weight {{W}} N down; normal {{N}} N perpendicular to the plank; friction {{f}} N up the plank.

hints.text: What touches the block? Only the plank. Gravity acts too. The plank can push perpendicular to its surface and along it.
The block is at rest: the net force is zero. Tilt the axes and balance along and across the plank.
Across: N = mg cos θ. Along: friction up the slope = mg sin θ.

normal-equals-weight.text: On a slope the plank pushes back only against the part of the weight pressing into it: N = mg cos θ, not mg.

extra-force-of-motion.text: Nothing pushes the block down the slope except gravity, and gravity is already the weight. The pull down the slope is just the weight's component, not an extra force.

static-friction-always-max.text: Static friction is only as large as needed to stop slipping: here it balances mg sin θ.

friction-direction-opposes-force.text: The block would slide down, so friction acts up the slope.

missing-weight.text: Every body near the Earth has a weight, mg, straight down.

missing-normal.text: The plank pushes on the block perpendicular to its surface.

missing-friction.text: Without friction the block would slide down. The rough plank holds it.

normal-direction.text: The normal force is perpendicular to the plank, not straight up.

double-counted-force.text: The plank gives one normal force and one friction force. Remove the duplicate.

generic.text: Name the agent of each arrow (Earth, plank) and check that the net force is zero.

workedSolution.text: Weight {{W}} N straight down, from the Earth.
Tilted axes. Across the plank: N = mg cos {{theta}}° = {{N}} N.
Along the plank: friction balances mg sin {{theta}}° = {{f}} N, up the slope. Press Play: the block stays still.

generic.front: Forces on a block resting on a rough slope?
generic.back: Weight (down), normal mg cos θ (perpendicular), static friction mg sin θ (up the slope).

reasoning.prompt: In one or two sentences, explain why the friction force here is mg sin θ and not μs N.
rubric: Says the block is at rest, so the net force along the plank is zero
Names mg sin θ as the component of the weight along the plank
Explains that μs N is only the maximum static friction
Compares the friction needed with the friction available
reasoning.modelAnswer: The block isn't moving, so the forces along the plank balance and friction equals the component of the weight down the plank, mg sin θ. μs N is only the largest friction the surface can supply; here {{fmax}} N is available but only {{f}} N is needed.

template.intro: This question helps us find the best place for you to begin.
stem: A {{m}} kg block rests on a rough plank tilted at {{theta}}°. The coefficient of static friction is {{muS}}. Take g = 9.8 m/s².
What is the magnitude of the friction force acting on the block?

hints.text: Is the block moving? What does that tell you about the net force along the plank?
Turn on tilted axes. Which forces have a component along the plank?
Along the plank, friction must exactly balance mg sin θ. μs N is only the most friction could be.

static-friction-always-max.text: You found the maximum static friction, μs N. The block isn't slipping, so friction is only as large as it needs to be. With your value the block would accelerate, as the simulation shows. The meter compares what is needed with what is available.

normal-equals-weight.text: On an incline the plank pushes back only against the part of the weight pressing into it: N = mg cos θ, not mg.

sin-cos-swap-incline.text: Check which component points along the plank. The angle between the weight and the plank's normal is θ, so the component along the plank is mg sin θ.

dimension-mismatch.text: Friction is a force. Check your units.

generic.text: Compare the forces along the plank. What has to balance for the block to stay still? Watch what your value would do.

workedSolution.text: The block is at rest, so the net force along the plank is zero. Resolve the weight along tilted axes.
Across the plank: N = mg cos θ = {{N}} N.
Along the plank: static friction balances mg sin θ, so f = {{m}} × 9.8 × sin {{theta}}° = {{f}} N. Press Play: the block stays put.
Check: the most friction available is μs N = {{fmax}} N, more than the {{f}} N needed, so the block indeed doesn't slip.

static-friction-always-max.front: Is static friction always μs N?
static-friction-always-max.back: No. μs N is the maximum. Static friction is only as large as needed to prevent slipping.

normal-equals-weight.front: On a θ incline, is the normal force on a resting block equal to its weight?
normal-equals-weight.back: No. It balances only the component of weight into the surface: N = mg cos θ.

sin-cos-swap-incline.front: Which component of weight acts along a slope of angle θ?
sin-cos-swap-incline.back: mg sin θ along the slope; mg cos θ perpendicular to it.

generic.front: Friction on a block resting on an incline?
generic.back: f = mg sin θ (as long as that is no more than μs mg cos θ).

stem: A {{m}} kg crate is dragged across a rough floor at a constant speed by a horizontal rope. The coefficient of kinetic friction is {{mu}}. Take g = 9.8 m/s².
What is the tension in the rope?

hints.text: Constant speed: what is the net force? Press Play with different pulls.
Horizontally, the rope's pull balances kinetic friction. Kinetic friction = μ_k N.
N = mg on a level floor, so T = μ_k m g.

mass-instead-of-weight.text: Friction is μ times the normal force, which is a force (m g, in newtons), not the mass.

tension-equals-weight.text: The rope is horizontal: it balances friction, not the weight. The floor holds the weight up. Watch your value: the crate speeds up.

dimension-mismatch.text: Tension is a force, in newtons.

generic.text: At constant speed the forces balance: tension = kinetic friction.

workedSolution.text: Vertically: N = m g = {{W}} N.
Constant speed, so horizontally T = μ_k N = {{mu}} × {{W}} = {{T}} N. Press Play: the speed stays steady.

mass-instead-of-weight.back: μ_k m g: μ times the normal force, a force in newtons.

template.intro: A quick check on momentum.
stem: A {{M}} kg gun, at rest, fires a {{mb}} g bullet at {{vb}} m/s.
With what speed does the gun recoil?

hints.text: Before firing, nothing moves: the total momentum is zero. What must it be just after?
The bullet's momentum forwards must be cancelled by the gun's momentum backwards: m_bullet × v_bullet = M_gun × V.
Convert the bullet's mass to kilograms first, then divide its momentum by the gun's mass.

recoil-same-speed.text: Equal and opposite momenta, not speeds. The gun is far heavier, so it moves far more slowly.

momentum-not-velocity.text: That is the bullet's momentum (in kg m/s). The gun has the same momentum backwards; divide by its mass to get its speed.

mass-ratio-inverted.text: The heavier body moves more slowly: V = m v ÷ M, with the small mass on top.

dimension-mismatch.text: A recoil speed is a velocity, in m/s.

generic.text: Total momentum stays zero: m v forwards for the bullet equals M V backwards for the gun.

workedSolution.text: Before: total momentum 0. After: bullet {{mbkg}} kg × {{vb}} m/s = {{pb}} kg m/s forwards.
The gun carries {{pb}} kg m/s backwards, so V = {{pb}} ÷ {{M}} = {{V}} m/s.

recoil-same-speed.front: A gun fires a bullet. Do they move apart at the same speed?
recoil-same-speed.back: No. Their momenta are equal and opposite; the heavy gun moves slowly.

momentum-not-velocity.front: Momentum or velocity: which is shared equally (and oppositely) in a recoil?
momentum-not-velocity.back: Momentum. Divide by each mass to find each speed.

mass-ratio-inverted.front: Recoil speed of a gun of mass M firing mass m at v?

generic.front: Recoil from rest?
generic.back: m v = M V: total momentum stays zero.

template.intro: Directions matter in this one.
stem: Cart A ({{m1}} kg) moves right at {{u1}} m/s. Cart B ({{m2}} kg) moves left at {{absU2}} m/s. They collide head-on and stick together.
What is their velocity just after the collision? Take rightward as positive (give a negative value for leftward).

hints.text: Momentum is a vector. With rightward positive, what sign does cart B's velocity have?
Total momentum before = m_A u_A + m_B u_B, with u_B negative. It is the same just after.
Divide the total momentum by the total mass; the sign tells you the direction.

momentum-direction-ignored.text: You added the momenta as if both carts moved the same way. Cart B moves left, so its momentum is negative and partly cancels A's.

averages-velocities.text: Averaging velocities ignores the masses. Use total momentum ÷ total mass.

sign-error.text: Check the direction: compare the size of A's rightward momentum with B's leftward momentum.

dimension-mismatch.text: Give a velocity in m/s.

generic.text: Write each momentum with its sign, add them, and divide by the total mass.

workedSolution.text: Rightward positive: p_A = {{m1}} × {{u1}} = {{p1}} kg m/s; p_B = {{m2}} × ({{u2}}) = {{p2}} kg m/s.
Total: {{ptot}} kg m/s, shared by {{M}} kg after sticking: v = {{ptot}} ÷ {{M}} = {{v}} m/s, so the pair moves {{dir}}.

momentum-direction-ignored.front: Two carts move towards each other. Do their momenta add?
momentum-direction-ignored.back: They partly cancel: momentum is a vector, so give each a sign.

averages-velocities.front: Two carts stick together. Is their speed the average of the two speeds?
averages-velocities.back: No. Use momentum: (m₁ + m₂) v = m₁u₁ + m₂u₂.

generic.front: Head-on sticking collision?
generic.back: v = (m₁u₁ + m₂u₂) ÷ (m₁ + m₂), with signs for direction.

template.intro: Two carts, one collision.
stem: Cart A ({{m1}} kg) rolls at {{u1}} m/s and hits cart B ({{m2}} kg), which is at rest. The carts stick together.
How fast do they move just after the collision?

hints.text: During the collision the carts push on each other equally and oppositely, so their total momentum doesn't change.
Momentum before = m_A × u_A (B is at rest). After, both carts move together with one shared speed.
(m_A + m_B) v = m_A u_A. Divide by the total mass.

averages-velocities.text: Averaging the speeds ignores the masses. Momentum is shared: (m_A + m_B) v = m_A u_A.

velocity-unchanged.text: Cart A now has to drag cart B along, so the pair moves more slowly than A did. Watch your value: momentum would grow.

wrong-mass-after-collision.text: After sticking, both masses move together: divide by m_A + m_B, not by one cart's mass.

dimension-mismatch.text: Give a speed in m/s.

generic.text: Write momentum before and after; the total is conserved.

workedSolution.text: Before: p = {{m1}} × {{u1}} = {{p1}} kg m/s (cart B has none).
After: both carts, {{M}} kg in all, move together at v. Conservation: {{M}} v = {{p1}}, so v = {{v}} m/s.

averages-velocities.front: Two carts stick together. Is their speed the average of the two speeds?
averages-velocities.back: No. Use momentum: (m₁ + m₂) v = m₁u₁ + m₂u₂.

velocity-unchanged.front: A moving cart sticks to one at rest. Same speed afterwards?
velocity-unchanged.back: No, slower: the same momentum is shared by more mass.

wrong-mass-after-collision.front: After a sticking collision, which mass moves?

template.intro: A quick check on splitting a force into parts.
stem: A block on a slope inclined at {{theta}}° has a weight of {{W}} N.
What is the component of its weight along the slope (down the slope)?

hints.text: Turn on the tilted axes: one runs along the slope, the other straight out of it.
The angle between the weight and the line perpendicular to the slope equals the slope angle θ. Which side of that triangle lies along the slope?
The part along the slope is opposite θ in the triangle, so it is W sin θ.

sin-cos-swap-incline.text: That is the part pressing into the slope, W cos θ. The angle θ sits between the weight and the slope's perpendicular, so the part along the slope is the side opposite θ: W sin θ.

whole-weight-along-slope.text: Only part of the weight acts along the slope; the rest presses into it. Split the weight along the tilted axes.

dimension-mismatch.text: A component of a force is itself a force, in newtons.

generic.text: Split the weight along the slope and perpendicular to it, then pick the part that lies along the slope.

workedSolution.text: Use axes along and perpendicular to the slope.
The angle between the weight and the perpendicular to the slope is θ = {{theta}}°, so along the slope: W sin θ = {{W}} × sin {{theta}}° = {{along}} N.
Into the slope: W cos θ = {{perp}} N. Together the two parts rebuild the {{W}} N weight.

sin-cos-swap-incline.front: Which component of weight acts along a slope of angle θ?
sin-cos-swap-incline.back: W sin θ along the slope; W cos θ into it.

whole-weight-along-slope.front: Does all of a block's weight pull it down a slope?
whole-weight-along-slope.back: No. Only W sin θ acts along the slope; W cos θ presses into it.

generic.front: Weight component along a θ slope?

template.intro: A harder one: the push is not along the slope.
stem: A {{m}} kg block rests on a smooth plank tilted at {{theta}}°. It is held still by a horizontal push F (pointing towards the slope). Take g = 9.8 m/s².
How large must F be?

hints.text: Along the slope only two forces have parts: the weight and the push. Which way does each part point?
The horizontal push makes angle θ with the slope, so its part up the slope is F cos θ. The weight's part down the slope is mg sin θ.
Balance them: F cos θ = mg sin θ, so F = mg tan θ.

horizontal-push-treated-as-parallel.text: You treated the push as if it acted along the slope. It is horizontal, so only F cos θ of it acts up the slope. Play your value: the block slides.

sin-cos-swap-incline.text: Check which part of the weight acts along the slope: mg sin θ, not mg cos θ.

tan-inverted.text: Your ratio is upside down. F cos θ = mg sin θ gives F = mg sin θ ÷ cos θ = mg tan θ.

dimension-mismatch.text: F is a force: give it in newtons.

generic.text: Resolve along the slope: the push's part up the slope must balance the weight's part down it. Watch what your value does.

workedSolution.text: Resolve along the slope (tilted axes). The normal force has no part along it.
Weight down the slope: mg sin {{theta}}° = {{along}} N. Push up the slope: F cos {{theta}}°.
At rest these balance: F = mg tan {{theta}}° = {{F}} N. Press Play: the block stays still.

horizontal-push-treated-as-parallel.front: A horizontal push F on a θ slope: how much acts along the slope?
horizontal-push-treated-as-parallel.back: F cos θ (and F sin θ presses into the slope).

sin-cos-swap-incline.front: Which component of weight acts along a slope of angle θ?
sin-cos-swap-incline.back: mg sin θ along the slope; mg cos θ perpendicular to it.

tan-inverted.front: F cos θ = mg sin θ. What is F?

generic.front: Smooth slope, horizontal push holding a block still?

template.intro: Build the diagram, then let the model test it.
stem: A {{m}} kg block is pushed up a smooth (frictionless) plank tilted at {{theta}}°. Your hand pushes parallel to the plank and the block moves up at a constant speed. Take g = 9.8 m/s².
Draw every force acting on the block, with its size and direction.
template.answerText: Weight {{W}} N down; normal {{N}} N perpendicular to the plank; push {{P}} N up the plank.

hints.text: What touches the block? The plank and your hand. Gravity acts too. Is anything else pushing it?
Constant speed means the net force is zero. Tilt the axes and balance the forces along and across the plank.
Across the plank: N = mg cos θ. Along it: push = mg sin θ. There is no separate force for the motion itself.

extra-force-of-motion.text: There is no separate 'force of motion'. The block keeps moving at a steady speed because the forces balance. Ask of each arrow: what is pushing or pulling?

args.text: Every force needs an agent: Earth, plank or hand.

normal-equals-weight.text: On a slope the plank pushes back only against the part of the weight pressing into it: N = mg cos θ, not mg.

constant-velocity-unbalanced.text: At constant speed the push along the plank must exactly balance the weight's component down the plank, mg sin θ. Your diagram predicts the block speeding up or slowing down.

missing-weight.text: Every body near the Earth has a weight, mg, straight down.

missing-normal.text: The plank pushes on the block, perpendicular to its surface. Without it the block would sink into the plank.

missing-push.text: Your hand pushes the block up along the plank.

normal-direction.text: The normal force is perpendicular to the plank, not straight up.

push-direction.text: The push is parallel to the plank, up the slope.

double-counted-force.text: Each agent here gives one force. Remove the duplicate.

generic.text: List the agents (Earth, plank, hand), give each one force, and check that the net force is zero for a steady speed.

workedSolution.text: Weight: {{W}} N straight down, from the Earth.
Use axes along and across the plank. Across it, nothing accelerates: N = mg cos {{theta}}° = {{N}} N.
Along it, the speed is constant, so the push balances mg sin {{theta}}° = {{P}} N. No other force acts; press Play to see the steady motion.

generic.front: A block pushed up a smooth slope at constant speed: which forces act?
generic.back: Weight (down), normal (perpendicular to the slope) and the push (along it). No 'force of motion'.

template.intro: A quick check on F = ma.
stem: A net force of {{F}} N acts on a {{m}} kg cart.
What is its acceleration?

hints.text: Newton's second law links net force, mass and acceleration.
F = m a. Which quantity are you finding?
a = F ÷ m.

force-times-mass.text: Multiplying gives units of kg N. A bigger mass should make the acceleration smaller: a = F ÷ m.

second-law-inverted.text: Your ratio is upside down: a larger force must give a larger acceleration, so a = F ÷ m.

dimension-mismatch.text: Acceleration is in m/s².

generic.text: Use F = m a and rearrange for a.

workedSolution.text: Newton's second law: F = m a, so a = F ÷ m.

force-times-mass.front: Net force F on mass m: acceleration?
force-times-mass.back: a = F ÷ m, not F × m.

second-law-inverted.front: Doubling the force on a body does what to its acceleration?

generic.front: Newton's second law?

args.text: Impulse is the change in momentum, with direction.

template.intro: Impulse, with a change of direction.
stem: A {{m}} g ball hits a wall at {{u}} m/s and bounces straight back at {{v}} m/s.
What is the magnitude of the impulse the wall gives the ball?

hints.text: Impulse equals the change in momentum. Momentum has a direction: choose one direction as positive.
Taking the bounce-back direction as positive, the momentum before is negative and after is positive.
Change = m v − (−m u) = m (u + v).

momentum-direction-ignored.text: You subtracted the speeds as if the ball kept going the same way. It reverses, so the change is m(u + v), not m(u − v).

impulse-one-velocity.text: That is only the momentum before. The wall first stops the ball and then sends it back, so both momenta count.

dimension-mismatch.text: Impulse is in N s (the same as kg m/s).

generic.text: Impulse = change in momentum. Take signs for the two directions.

workedSolution.text: Take the bounce-back direction as positive. Before: p = −{{mkg}} × {{u}} = −{{pin}} kg m/s.
After: p = +{{mkg}} × {{v}} = {{pout}} kg m/s.
Impulse = change in momentum = {{pout}} − (−{{pin}}) = {{J}} N s, away from the wall.

momentum-direction-ignored.front: A ball bounces straight back. Is the momentum change m(u − v)?
momentum-direction-ignored.back: No: m(u + v). The direction reverses.

impulse-one-velocity.front: Impulse on a bouncing ball: only the incoming momentum?
impulse-one-velocity.back: No. Impulse = final momentum − initial momentum, both with signs.

generic.front: Impulse?

template.intro: This question helps us find the best place for you to begin.
stem: Four carts start from rest on a smooth track. Each is pulled by a steady force.
Put them in order of acceleration, greatest first.

hints.text: Newton's second law links force, mass and acceleration. Which one do you need to compare?
Work out a = F ÷ m for each cart.
Cart P: {{FP}} ÷ {{mP}}. Do the same for Q, R and S, then order them.

ignores-mass.text: You ordered the carts by force alone. The race now gives every cart the same mass, so only the force matters: that is the world your order describes. Real carts differ in mass, and a heavier cart needs more force for the same acceleration: compare F ÷ m.

args.text: Race with every cart given the same 2 kg mass.

ignores-force.text: You ordered the carts by mass alone. The race now pulls every cart with the same force, so only the mass matters: that is the world your order describes. Real carts are pulled by different forces, and a bigger force can outweigh a bigger mass: compare F ÷ m.

args.text: Race with every cart pulled by the same 6 N force.

reversed-order.text: That's the reverse order: greatest acceleration goes first.

generic.text: Compare a = F ÷ m for each cart, then order them.

workedSolution.text: Newton's second law: a = F ÷ m.
P: {{aP}} m/s²; Q: {{aQ}} m/s²; R: {{aR}} m/s²; S: {{aS}} m/s².
Greatest first: {{order}}.

ignores-mass.front: Cart X: 8 N on 4 kg. Cart Y: 6 N on 2 kg. Which accelerates faster?
ignores-mass.back: Y: 3 m/s² against 2 m/s². Compare F/m, not F alone.

ignores-force.front: Does the lightest cart always accelerate fastest?
ignores-force.back: No. a = F/m: a larger force can beat a smaller mass.

generic.front: Newton's second law for acceleration?

template.intro: A quick check on action and reaction.
stem: A book rests on a table. Its weight is the Earth's gravitational pull on the book.
By Newton's third law, what is the partner (reaction) of this force?
template.answerText: The book's pull on the Earth

hints.text: A third-law pair is one interaction between two bodies: if A acts on B, the partner is B acting on A.
Here A is the Earth, B is the book, and the interaction is gravity.
Swap the roles: the book pulls the Earth by gravity.

third-law-pair-on-same-body.text: Both of these act on the book, so they can't be a third-law pair. They balance because the book is at rest (first law), not because of the third law.

third-law-wrong-interaction.text: The book's push on the table is the partner of the table's push on the book (a contact interaction). The weight's partner is also gravitational.

third-law-only-when-moving.text: Third-law pairs exist whenever two bodies interact, moving or not.

generic.text: Swap the two bodies and keep the same kind of interaction.

workedSolution.text: The weight is a gravitational force: Earth on book.
Its partner is the same interaction the other way round: book on Earth, upwards, equal in size ({{W}} N). It acts on the Earth, so it isn't on this board.

third-law-pair-on-same-body.front: Are weight and normal force on a book an action–reaction pair?
third-law-pair-on-same-body.back: No. Third-law pairs act on different bodies. The pair of the book's weight is the book's pull on the Earth.

third-law-wrong-interaction.front: The partner of a gravitational force is…?
third-law-wrong-interaction.back: Another gravitational force, on the other body.

third-law-only-when-moving.back: No: any interaction between two bodies gives a pair.

generic.front: Third-law partner of 'Earth pulls book'?

options.text: The book's gravitational pull on the Earth, upwards
The table's upward push on the book
The book's push down on the table
There is none, because the book isn't moving

args.text: Third-law forces are equal in size whatever the masses.

template.intro: Same force, different bodies.
stem: A {{M}} kg truck and a {{m}} kg car collide head-on. At one instant the truck pushes on the car with a force of {{F}} N.
At that instant, how large is the force the car exerts on the truck?

hints.text: The two forces are one interaction between the truck and the car.
Newton's third law doesn't depend on mass or on who is 'stronger'. The masses change the accelerations, not the forces.
The car pushes back on the truck with an equal force in the opposite direction.

heavier-pushes-harder.text: The masses don't change the size of a third-law pair. They change the accelerations: the car accelerates more because it is lighter.

third-law-forces-cancel.text: The two forces act on different bodies, so they never cancel each other. Each one changes the motion of the body it acts on.

dimension-mismatch.text: Give a force, in newtons.

generic.text: Use Newton's third law: equal in size, opposite in direction, on the other body.

workedSolution.text: The truck pushing the car and the car pushing the truck are a third-law pair.
So the car pushes on the truck with {{F}} N, backwards. The car's acceleration is {{F}} ÷ {{m}} = {{ac}} m/s²; the truck's only {{F}} ÷ {{M}} = {{at}} m/s².

heavier-pushes-harder.front: In a truck–car collision, which pushes harder on the other?
heavier-pushes-harder.back: Neither: the forces are equal and opposite. The car accelerates more because it is lighter.

third-law-forces-cancel.front: Do the two forces of a third-law pair cancel?
third-law-forces-cancel.back: No. They act on different bodies.

generic.front: Third law in a collision?
generic.back: Equal and opposite forces on the two bodies, whatever their masses.

template.intro: This question helps us find the best place for you to begin.
stem: A {{m}} kg book rests on a table.
Which of these are Newton's third-law (action–reaction) pairs? Choose every correct pair.
template.answerText: The Earth–book gravitational pair and the table–book contact pair

hints.text: An action–reaction pair comes from one interaction between two bodies.
The two forces of a pair act on different bodies, so they can never cancel each other.
Gravity pair: Earth on book and book on Earth. Contact pair: table on book and book on table.

third-law-pair-on-same-body.text: The weight and the normal force both act on the book, so they are not a third-law pair. They balance here because the book is at rest, by Newton's first law.

third-law-different-interaction.text: A third-law pair is one interaction seen from both sides: the same kind of force, acting on the two bodies involved. These two forces come from different interactions.

missed-correct-option.text: There is more than one pair. Look for each interaction: gravity between the Earth and the book, and contact between the table and the book.

generic.text: For each option, ask: is it one interaction between two bodies, with one force on each?

workedSolution.text: Gravity: the Earth pulls the book down and the book pulls the Earth up, with equal size {{W}} N. That is one pair.
Contact: the table pushes the book up and the book pushes the table down, with equal size. That is the second pair.
The weight and the normal force both act on the book. They balance because the book is at rest, not because of the third law.

third-law-pair-on-same-body.front: Are weight and normal force on a book an action–reaction pair?
third-law-pair-on-same-body.back: No. Third-law pairs act on different bodies. The pair of the book's weight is the book's pull on the Earth.

third-law-different-interaction.front: What do the two forces of a third-law pair have in common?
third-law-different-interaction.back: Same interaction and type, equal size, opposite directions, acting on the two different bodies.

generic.front: How do you find a force's third-law partner?
generic.back: Swap the bodies: 'A on B' pairs with 'B on A', same kind of force.

options.text: The Earth pulls the book down; the book pulls the Earth up
The table pushes the book up; the book pushes the table down
The Earth pulls the book down; the table pushes the book up

template.intro: This question helps us find the best place for you to begin.
stem: A ball is kicked from level ground at {{v}} m/s, {{ang}}° above the horizontal. Ignore air resistance and take g = 9.8 m/s².
How far away does it land?

hints.text: Treat the horizontal and vertical motions separately. Which one decides how long the ball is in the air? Watch the two graphs as the ball flies.
Time of flight: t = 2u sin θ ÷ g. Horizontal speed stays u cos θ.
Range = u cos θ × 2u sin θ ÷ g = u² sin 2θ ÷ g.

forgot-double-angle.text: The range uses sin 2θ, not sin θ: it comes from 2 sin θ cos θ, the time of flight times the horizontal speed.

used-time-to-apex.text: That's the distance covered while rising to the top: half the flight. The ball takes as long again to come down.

ignored-horizontal-component.text: Only the horizontal component u cos θ carries the ball sideways. The full speed u points partly upward.

dimension-mismatch.text: Range is a distance. Check your unit.

generic.text: Split the motion: the time in the air comes from the vertical part, the distance from the horizontal part. The coral flag marks your answer.

workedSolution.text: Horizontal speed: u cos θ = {{v}} cos {{ang}}° = {{vx}} m/s. It doesn't change.
Time of flight: t = 2u sin θ ÷ g = {{tf}} s.
Range = {{vx}} × {{tf}} = {{R}} m.

forgot-double-angle.front: Range of a projectile on level ground?

used-time-to-apex.front: Is the time to the top the whole flight time?
used-time-to-apex.back: No, it's half of it (on level ground).

ignored-horizontal-component.front: Which velocity component carries a projectile sideways?
ignored-horizontal-component.back: The horizontal one, u cos θ, constant without air resistance.

generic.front: How do you find a projectile's range?

template.intro: A quick check on components.
stem: A {{F}} N force acts at {{ang}}° above the +x axis. The force and its two components form a right triangle.
Which side of that triangle is adjacent to the {{ang}}° angle?

hints.text: The adjacent side touches the angle but is not the longest side.
The angle sits between the force and the x-axis. Which two sides meet there?
The force is the hypotenuse; the other side touching the angle is the x-component.

opposite-adjacent-confusion.text: The vertical side is across from the angle: it is opposite. The side that touches the angle, along the x-axis, is adjacent.

hypotenuse-confusion.text: The force is the longest side, the hypotenuse. Adjacent means the other side that touches the angle.

generic.text: Find the two sides that meet at the angle; the shorter one is adjacent.

workedSolution.text: Draw the force's shadows on the axes: those are its components.
The {{ang}}° angle is between the force and the x-axis, so the x-component is adjacent and the y-component is opposite.

opposite-adjacent-confusion.front: In a right triangle, which side is adjacent to an angle?
opposite-adjacent-confusion.back: The side that touches the angle and isn't the hypotenuse. The opposite side is across from it.

hypotenuse-confusion.back: No: the hypotenuse is the longest side, opposite the right angle.

generic.front: Force at θ above the x-axis: which component is adjacent to θ?

options.text: The x-component, along the x-axis
The y-component, vertical
The force itself

template.intro: Here the angle is measured from north.
stem: A {{F}} N force acts at {{alpha}}° west of north. Take east as +x and north as +y.
What is its x-component? Include the sign.

hints.text: Sketch it: the force leans left of the north axis. Which way does its x-component point?
The given angle is measured from the y-axis, so the x-component is the side opposite that angle.
F_x = −F sin α (negative, because it points west).

component-sign-dropped.text: The size is right, but the force leans west, so its x-component is negative.

sin-cos-swap.text: The angle is measured from north, not from the x-axis. The x-component is opposite that angle: F sin α, with a minus sign for west.

tan-for-component.text: tan relates the two components to each other. Use sin α for the side opposite the angle.

sign-error.text: Check the direction: west of north means the force has a westward (negative x) part.

dimension-mismatch.text: A component of a force is a force, in newtons.

generic.text: Find which side is opposite the {{alpha}}° angle, then decide its sign.

workedSolution.text: The force is {{alpha}}° from the +y axis, leaning west.
The x-component is opposite the angle: size F sin α = {{F}} × sin {{alpha}}° = {{mag}} N. It points west, so F_x = {{Fx}} N (and F_y = +{{Fy}} N).

component-sign-dropped.front: A force points west of north. Sign of its x-component (east positive)?

sin-cos-swap.front: Force F at θ above the x-axis: x-component?
sin-cos-swap.back: F cos θ (adjacent). The y-component is F sin θ.

tan-for-component.front: Does F tan θ give a component of F?
tan-for-component.back: No. tan θ = F_y ÷ F_x relates the components to each other.

generic.front: Angle measured from the y-axis: which ratio gives F_x?
generic.back: sin (the x-component is opposite that angle).

template.intro: Splitting a force into components.
stem: A {{F}} N force acts at {{ang}}° above the +x axis.
What is its x-component?

hints.text: The force is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with its two components.
The x-component is the side adjacent to the {{ang}}° angle. Which ratio links adjacent and hypotenuse?
Adjacent = hypotenuse × cos θ, so F_x = F cos θ.

sin-cos-swap.text: You found the side opposite the angle, the y-component. The x-component is adjacent to the angle: F cos θ.

tan-for-component.text: tan θ relates the two components to each other, not a component to the force. Use cos θ for the adjacent side.

dimension-mismatch.text: A component of a force is a force, in newtons.

generic.text: Identify the side adjacent to the angle and use the matching ratio.

workedSolution.text: Split F into components along the axes.
The x-component is adjacent to {{ang}}°: F_x = {{F}} × cos {{ang}}° = {{Fx}} N. (The y-component is {{Fy}} N.)

sin-cos-swap.front: Force F at θ above the x-axis: x-component?
sin-cos-swap.back: F cos θ (adjacent). The y-component is F sin θ.

tan-for-component.front: Does F tan θ give a component of F?
tan-for-component.back: No. tan θ = F_y ÷ F_x relates the components to each other.

generic.front: x-component of a force at θ above +x?

template.intro: Adding vectors that point different ways.
stem: Vector a has magnitude {{a}} units pointing east. Vector b has magnitude {{b}} units pointing north.
What is the magnitude of a + b?

hints.text: Place b's tail at a's tip. The resultant runs from a's tail to b's tip.
The two vectors are at right angles, so they form the two shorter sides of a right triangle.
